{{Short description|18th century English mathematician, clergyman, and philosopher}}
'''John Rowning''' (c. 1701 – November 1771) was an English mathematician, clergyman, and philosopher. He wrote on natural philosophy, designed measuring and calculating instruments. In his book he rejected the idea of Newtonian ether and explained gravitational forces as being the action of God. 

Rowning was the son of a namesake from [[Ashby cum Fenby|Ashby-with-Fenby, Lincolnshire]] who may have been a watchmaker as a brother took to the profession. He was educated in [[Brigg|Glanford Brigg]] before joining [[Magdalene College, Cambridge]] as a [[sizar]], graduating BA in 1724 and MA four years later. He become a teacher of experimental philosophy while also working with William Deane on the design of philosophical instruments. He designed a barometer with alterable accuracy using tubes of varying diameters in 1733.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rowning |first=John |date=1733-12-31 |title=V. A description of a barometer, wherin the scale of variation may be encreased at pleasure |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London |language=en |volume=38 |issue=427 |pages=39–42 |doi=10.1098/rstl.1733.0005 |issn=0261-0523|doi-access=free }}</ref> He also wrote on graphical solutions to parabolic equations.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Rowning |first=John |date=1771-12-31 |title=XXIV. Directions for making a machine for finding the roots of equations universally, with the manner of using it |url=https://royalsocietypublishing.org/doi/10.1098/rstl.1770.0024 |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London |language=en |volume=60 |pages=240–256 |doi=10.1098/rstl.1770.0024 |issn=0261-0523|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He was made rector at Westley Waterless, Cambridgeshire in 1734 and later at Anderby. He published ''A Compendious System of Natural Philosophy'' which went through revisions from 1735 to 1772. Rowning believed that matter could both attract and repel and included examples of  cohesion of mercury drops, other liquids, capillary rise and suggested that attractive forces worked at short ranges and that they begin to repel after a certain range.<ref>{{cite book |author=Rowlinson, J.S. |title=Cohesion: A Scientific History of Intermolecular Forces |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2005 |pages=21–25}}</ref> [[Joseph Priestley]] was educated at Daventry Academy where Rowning's text was used and he followed the idea that particles could attract or repel depending on the distance in some of his views on optics.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Schofield, R.E. |year=2005 |title=Joseph Priestley, Natural Philosopher |url=http://acshist.scs.illinois.edu/bulletin_open_access/v30-2/v30-2%20p57-62.pdf |journal=Bull. Hist. Chem. |volume=30 |issue=2 |pages=57–62|doi=10.70359/bhc2005v030p057 }}</ref> Rowning believed that the brightness of stars varied only due to the distance from the earth.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=McCormmach |first=Russell |date=1968 |title=John Michell and Henry Cavendish: Weighing the Stars |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/product/identifier/S0007087400003459/type/journal_article |journal=The British Journal for the History of Science |language=en |volume=4 |issue=2 |pages=126–155 |doi=10.1017/S0007087400003459 |issn=0007-0874|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He was a member and sometime secretary of the Gentleman's Society of Spalding.<ref>{{Cite ODNB|author=McConnell, Anita |title=The Oxford Dictionary of National Biography |date=2004-09-23 |url=http://www.oxforddnb.com/view/article/24230 |chapter=Rowning, John |pages=ref:odnb/24230 |editor-last=Matthew |editor-first=H. C. G. |place=Oxford |doi=10.1093/ref:odnb/24230 |access-date=2022-07-06 |editor2-last=Harrison |editor2-first=B.}}</ref> 

He was married and had three sons and a daughter. He died at his home on [[Carey Street]] in London.
